analysis.one_liner: Postpones the scheduled minimum wage increase to $7.25 an hour by one year.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House subcommittee, and the minimum wage rose to $7.25 on schedule in July 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law was scheduled to raise the minimum wage from $6.55 to $7.25 an hour on July 24, 2009, the last step of a three-step increase passed in 2007. This bill would have pushed that final raise back a year, to July 24, 2010. Workers due the raise would have gone another year at $6.55; employers who pay minimum wage would have saved that difference. The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, businesses that pay minimum wage — restaurants, retail stores, and other labor-intensive employers — would have kept the difference between $6.55 and $7.25 for each minimum-wage worker for one year. For a full-time minimum-wage worker, the delayed raise was worth roughly $1,400 a year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Restaurants, retail, and other minimum-wage employers

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to move the effective date of the $7.25 minimum wage from July 24, 2009 to July 24, 2010, giving employers an additional year before paying the higher rate.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, minimum-wage workers — many in food service, retail, and caretaking jobs — would have gone a year without the 70-cent-an-hour raise they were already scheduled to receive under a law passed in 2007.

drawbacks.text: Full-time minimum-wage workers would have lost roughly $1,400 in wages over the delay, money that would have been spent in local economies.

During the 2009 recession, some employers argued that any cost increase, even a scheduled 70-cent raise, made it harder to keep staff on payroll; the bill's sponsor framed the delay as relief for employers facing a weak economy.
The delay would have applied nationwide, postponing a raise Congress had already enacted in 2007 and that workers and employers had three years to plan for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to employers — a one-year reprieve from a 70-cent wage increase — would have come directly out of the pay of the lowest-paid workers, at a time of high unemployment when those workers had little bargaining power. An honest accounting puts the worker cost ahead of the employer benefit: the raise had been law for two years, and businesses knew the date was coming.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Olson introduced the bill on July 23, 2009, just two days before the minimum wage was scheduled to rise to $7.25.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor, which was controlled by Democrats who had supported the 2007 minimum wage increase.
In October 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained with no hearings or markup recorded.
The bill died at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011, and the $7.25 minimum wage took effect on July 24, 2009 as originally scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Minimum-wage workers, who received their scheduled raise to $7.25 on time because the bill never moved; employers who would have benefited from the delay gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Minimum-wage workers who got their raise on schedule

for.name: Rep. Pete Olson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay the $7.25 minimum wage increase by one year.

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it sat in the Workforce Protections subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled committee that received the bill never acted on it.

industries.note: Minimum-wage-heavy employers would have saved the difference between $6.55 and $7.25 per hour for a year, a saving that comes directly out of workers' scheduled raises.
The one-year delay would have let these businesses postpone the final step of the 2007 wage increase, keeping labor costs lower at the expense of the lowest-paid workers.
